Despite the brevity of the excerpt, both Ilse and Jonas are drawn with impressive depth and complexity, avoiding one-dimensional stereotypes. 

Ilse appears stoic, stubborn, and deeply rooted in her manual, solitary life on the ferry, yet her internal reaction—holding her breath to see if Jonas will pick up the crank—reveals a quiet vulnerability and a lingering emotional investment in him. 

Similarly, Jonas initially presents as a stereotypical "city returnee" who has grown soft, wears a jacket, pulls a rolling suitcase, and dislikes getting his hands dirty. However, the author adds immediate complexity to him: his laugh is "not malicious, just tired," and despite his aversion to the grime and his alienated history (leaving at seventeen), he wordlessly removes his jacket, kneels on the wet planks, and tries to crank the engine. Neither character exists merely as a plot device; rather, the plot itself is driven entirely by their unspoken history and complex emotional dynamics.
